article.Citation: Greer G, Tolbert R. Subjective Reports of the Effects of MDMA in a Clinical Setting. Journal of Psychoactive Drugs. 1986.
article.Title: Subjective Reports of the Effects of MDMA in a Clinical Setting

ae_events.Description: Subject #14: week of increased appetite, 15 lb weight gain over a few weeks, later lost 10 lbs.
Subject #19: disabling anxiety attacks weeks post-session causing 7 missed workdays; entered long-term psychotherapy.
Subject #7 (high-dose): in-session nausea, vomiting, jaw tension, ataxia, urinary urgency, blurred vision, sweating, brief memory loss, brief hallucination/depth-perception distortion.
Subject #7: evening symptoms - appetite loss, vomiting, body odor, blurred vision, urinary urgency, mild hearing impairment, insomnia, cheek-biting during sleep.
Subject #7: jaw-opening difficulty persisting several days after session.
Subject #7: fatigue and hoarseness (2 days), one day unsteady on feet, brief visual illusion second night.
Jaw tension/shaking/teeth clenching during session in 22 subjects; 3 also next day; diazepam/propranolol relieved it in some.
Fatigue lasting hours to days post-session in 23 subjects; most resolved within 2 days.
Insomnia the night after session in 11 subjects.
Muscle aches/tightness in 8 subjects, mostly during session, some for a day after.
Loss of appetite during session in all but one subject; not reported as unpleasant.
Nausea during session in 7 subjects; some had stomach upset, appetite loss, or mild constipation 1-3 days after.
Difficulty walking during session, reported by 3 subjects.
Feeling cold during session reported as a problem by 2 subjects.
Sweating during session specifically noted by 2 subjects (common, mentioned only in passing).
One-off in-session symptoms (n=1 each): jittery vision, lip swelling, shakiness, numb hands and face.
Headache late in the session, reported by 1 subject.
Subject #16 fainted the evening of the session; author suggests psychosomatic cause, no further detail given.
Anorgasmia the day after session, reported by 1 subject.
Decreased sexual desire for one to two days, reported by 1 subject.
Transient elevated pulse/BP during session in 2 monitored subjects (e.g. pulse 60->112, BP 90/50->128/70).
Anxiety or nervousness during session, reported by 5 subjects (general cohort, excluding subject #19's later course).
Mild depression the day after session, reported by 2 subjects.
Mental fatigue for one day, reported by 1 subject.
Mild emotional inflation for one day, reported by 1 subject.
Feeling lonely or sad for brief periods during session, reported by 1 subject.
One to three minutes of fear and paranoia early in session, then flattened affect later that evening; 1 subject.
Subject #18: waves of physical and emotional "crud" during session and over following days, interpreted as "letting go."
Feeling simply more emotional after session, reported by 1 subject.
Subject #17: emotionally vulnerable/off-center for 3-4 days, including nonspecific anger two days after session.
Racing mind (1 subject) and confusion (1 subject) during the evening of their sessions.
Subject #6: hard to work the next day ("too much going on"), confused about relationship for two days.
Five to seven days of "negative self-talk," reported by 1 subject.

article.PosResult: Judged against the study's own framed primary outcome (subjective benefit from the MDMA session), the result is positive: every subject reported some benefit, all 29 described positive attitude/feeling changes, and all 9 subjects with DSM-III diagnoses reported significant relief (2 with full remission).
article.IsObservational: Naturalistic case series: 29 subjects self-/therapist-referred specifically for MDMA sessions in a clinical (non-research) practice, no randomization, and the authors explicitly state no placebo control group or double-blind assessment was conducted. Clearly observational, not RCT.
article.Condition: Coded '.' rather than Alcohol/Smoking/Opioid: subjects were referred for varied personal/therapeutic/relationship/spiritual purposes, not selected for or treated for an alcohol, smoking, or opioid use disorder. A secondary post-hoc finding (14/28 follow-up respondents reported decreased use of some mind-altering substance, including alcohol/marijuana/caffeine/tobacco/cocaine) is a general substance-use side-observation, not evidence this study targeted one of the three USPSTF conditions.
article.Corpus/Prefix: No explicit corpus/condition grouping label is stated in the article itself; coded '.'.
article.N: 29 is the number of subjects administered MDMA and reported on throughout Results/Discussion ("the first 29 people administered MDMA"; "MDMA was apparently physically safe for all 29 subjects"). Follow-up questionnaires were completed by only 28 of 29 (subject #22 sent a letter instead), but this does not change the analyzed N for demographics/AE purposes since subject #22's session data are still included.
article.AE_denominator: Set to 29 because the Undesirable Effects section states "All subjects reported some undesirable experience" and "Every subject reported some undesirable physical symptom," indicating AEs were assessed across the full N=29, not a narrower safety subset.
article.ArmScope: psychedelic_arm — single-arm naturalistic case series with no comparator group; all N/AE/demographic data derive from MDMA-exposed participants only.
article.PctFemale: No aggregate gender count or percentage is given anywhere in the article text; individual subjects' genders are inferable from pronouns (e.g. 'he'/'she') but never summed. The authors note underlying data are 'available from the authors in tabular form' but that table is not reproduced in this text. Coded '.'.
article.GenderCategory: Same as PctFemale — no breakdown reported in the article body, only scattered individual pronouns. Coded '.'.
article.PctBIPOC: No race/ethnicity information of any kind (aggregate or individual) is reported anywhere in the article text. Coded '.'.
article.PctIndigenous: Same as PctBIPOC — not reported. Coded '.'.
article.NumDistinctAEs: 33 distinct AE types were derived by the extractor from the narrative Results (Undesirable Effects, vital signs, and Discussion sections), since the article itself never states a single summary count of distinct AE types (it instead gives per-symptom subject counts, e.g. '23 subjects reported fatigue'). This required judgment-call consolidation: (1) subject #7's unusually long list of high-dose symptoms was grouped into ~4 thematic entries (AE03-AE06) rather than one row per symptom; (2) overlapping GI complaints (nausea, stomach upset, appetite loss, constipation) were consolidated into one 'nausea/GI' type (AE12) rather than split further. A different, defensible consolidation scheme would yield a different integer; treat 33 as an extractor-derived approximation, not an author-reported figure.
article.WorstSeverity: Severe, driven entirely by AE02 (subject #19's postsession disabling anxiety attacks/missed work). This conflicts with the authors' own summary statement, 'No side effects were serious and only one subject had a side effect last more than a week' — the authors did not label this event serious or assign it a formal grade. The Severe grade here is the extractor's rubric-based application of the FDA 'persistent or significant disability/incapacity' criterion (7 missed workdays, described by the authors themselves as 'disabling,' entry into long-term psychotherapy) and should be treated as a genuine judgment call flagged for human review, not an author-asserted seriousness label.

ae_events.Greer 1986_AE01: Onset coded 'delayed' (weeks+) because the clinically notable feature — 15 lb weight gain — accrued over 'a few weeks,' even though increased appetite itself began within the first week.
ae_events.Greer 1986_AE02: Graded Severe under the FDA 'persistent or significant disability/incapacity' criterion based on the authors' own characterization ('disabling') and the concrete functional impact (7 missed workdays) plus entry into long-term psychotherapy as an intervention. This is the single event driving article-level WorstSeverity=Severe and directly conflicts with the authors' aggregate claim that no side effects were serious — flagged for human review rather than silently accepted or silently downgraded.
ae_events.Greer 1986_AE03: AE_type set to 'both' because this consolidated entry mixes ordinary expected physical/sympathomimetic effects (nausea, jaw tension, ataxia, sweating) with a CEQ-sense perceptual event (brief depth-perception distortion with brief hallucination), which per the prompt's instructions should be flagged as challenging-experience phenomenology rather than folded silently into a plain AE count.
ae_events.Greer 1986_AE04: Consolidates several evening/post-session symptoms specific to subject #7's two high-dose sessions (200 mg single dose, 350 mg total — far above the standard 75-150 mg + 50 mg protocol) into one row rather than one row per symptom, given the number of distinct minor complaints listed for this one subject.
ae_events.Greer 1986_AE05: Graded Moderate (not Mild) because the jaw-opening difficulty is explicitly stated to have 'continued for several days,' meeting the rubric's Moderate criterion of functional impairment persisting beyond the dosing day.
ae_events.Greer 1986_AE06: AE_type set to 'both' because 'brief visual illusion' is a CEQ-sense perceptual event; consolidated with the co-occurring fatigue/hoarseness/unsteadiness for subject #7 to avoid over-fragmenting this one subject's post-session course into many single-item rows.
ae_events.Greer 1986_AE07: InterventionRequired coded 'N' as the modal answer even though the text states diazepam and propranolol 'clearly relieved' this effect in a subset (~4 of 22 subjects) — for the large majority no intervention is reported as required. Flagged because a stricter per-subject reading could justify 'Y' for that subset.
ae_events.Greer 1986_AE12: Consolidates in-session nausea (7 subjects) with related post-session GI complaints (stomach upset, appetite loss, mild constipation reported by smaller, overlapping subsets) into a single 'nausea/GI' AE type rather than 3-4 separate rows, since the article describes them as a continuum of the same underlying symptom cluster for overlapping subjects.
ae_events.Greer 1986_AE18: SeverityIndeterminate='Y' because the article gives no information on intervention, medical workup, or outcome beyond the author's speculative comment that it 'was psychosomatic' — insufficient detail to confidently grade beyond the rubric's Mild default for under-specified AEs. InterventionRequired coded '.' (not reported) for the same reason.
ae_events.Greer 1986_AE22: AE_type set to 'challenging_experience' (not plain AE) per the prompt's instruction that expected in-session anxiety/fear phenomenology should be flagged as CEQ-sense challenging experience rather than folded into a clinical AE count, since no intervention or escalation beyond the session is described for this general subgroup.
ae_events.Greer 1986_AE26: Classified as challenging_experience: transient in-session loneliness/sadness with no reported intervention or persistence, consistent with expected acute-dosing phenomenology.
ae_events.Greer 1986_AE27: Classified as challenging_experience: transient in-session fear/paranoia (1-3 minutes) with later flattened affect, resolved without intervention — expected acute phenomenology per the rubric's core adaptation principle.
ae_events.Greer 1986_AE28: AE_type set to 'both' given the subject's own description as mixed 'physical and emotional' and its extension over several days after the session, though ultimately self-interpreted positively ('letting go') and requiring no intervention.
ae_events.Greer 1986_AE30: Graded Moderate because the disturbance ('emotionally vulnerable and off center') is explicitly stated to last 3-4 days, meeting the rubric's Moderate threshold for functional/mood impairment persisting beyond the dosing day.
ae_events.Greer 1986_AE32: Graded Moderate because the impairment ('hard to work the next day') and confusion persisted 2 days beyond the session, meeting the rubric's Moderate criterion for impairment beyond the dosing day, despite no formal intervention being reported.
ae_events.Greer 1986_AE33: Graded Moderate because 5-7 days of persistent negative self-talk exceeds the dosing-day window and fits the rubric's Moderate example of 'low mood... lasting days to a few weeks,' even absent a reported intervention.
